title: Gosto de Lisboa — likes, dislikes and opinions
goal: Say what you like and dislike, in every shade, then give your opinion — while mastering one small preposition you must never forget: *de*.
bekal: using *gostar de* with all its contractions
building a scale from *adoro* down to *detesto*
using pronouns after prepositions: *para mim*, *contigo*, *com ele*

dialogs.title: Diálogo — No miradouro
dialogs.intro: Late afternoon at the Miradouro da Senhora do Monte. The city spreads out below, and the Tagus river glitters.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: I love it! I adore the viewpoints.

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.text: E de que é que gostas menos?
lines.id: And what do you like least?
lines.literal: and of what is it that you-like less?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Das ladeiras! Não gosto nada de subir.
lines.id: The hills! I don't like climbing at all.
lines.literal: of-the(pl) slopes! not I-like nothing of to-climb.

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.text: Pois, a cidade é toda a subir e a descer.
lines.id: Yeah, the whole city is up and down.
lines.literal: well, the city is all to climb and to descend.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Mas gosto muito da comida. O bacalhau é delicioso.
lines.id: But I really like the food. The salt cod is delicious.
lines.literal: but I-like much of-the food. the cod is delicious.

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.text: A sério? A maior parte dos estrangeiros não gosta.
lines.id: Really? Most foreigners don't like it.
lines.literal: in seriousness? the bigger part of-the(pl) foreigners not likes.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Eu acho que é ótimo. E tu, de que gostas mais aqui?
lines.id: I think it's great. And you, what do you like most here?
lines.literal: I I-find that is great. and you, of what you-like more here?

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.text: Gosto do rio. Ao fim da tarde é lindo.
lines.id: I like the river. Toward evening it's beautiful.
lines.literal: I-like of-the river. at-the end of-the afternoon is beautiful.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: I agree. And fado? Do you like it?

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.text: Gosto, mas prefiro música moderna. O fado é triste demais para mim.
lines.id: I do, but I prefer modern music. Fado is too sad for me.
lines.literal: I-like, but I-prefer music modern. the fado is sad too-much for me.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Para mim também é triste — mas gosto na mesma.
lines.id: It's sad for me too — but I like it anyway.
lines.literal: for me also is sad — but I-like in-the same.

notes: **Gostar never stands without de.** *Gosto de café*, *gostas de Lisboa*, *gostamos de ler*. And when the noun has an article, *de* contracts: *gosto **do** café*, *gosto **da** comida*, *gosto **dos** miradouros*. This is the most stubborn learner mistake — because English "like" takes its object directly, with nothing in between.

**Não gosto nada de...** means "I don't like ... at all", not "I don't like anything". Here *nada* strengthens the negation, just like "at all". Compare: *não gosto muito* (I don't really like it) and *não gosto nada* (I can't stand it).
**Adorar and detestar don't take de.** *Adoro os miradouros*, *detesto o frio*. Only *gostar* and *precisar* demand the preposition; their stronger relatives don't.

**Acho que...** is the most common way to give an opinion in Portugal — far more frequent than *penso que* or *na minha opinião*. The verb is *achar*, which literally means "to find". So the Portuguese "find" their opinion rather than "think" it — rather like English "I find that...".

**Para mim, not para eu.** After a preposition, pronouns change form: *mim*, *ti*, *si*, and so on — just as English says "for me", not "for I". It's one of the few places in Portuguese that demands a special form, and unfortunately it's used constantly.
**Na mesma** means "anyway" or "all the same" — a typically European Portuguese phrase not used in Brazil. *Está a chover, mas vou na mesma* = "it's raining, but I'm going anyway".

grammars.title: Gostar de and its contractions
body: The verb itself is completely regular. What needs practice is what comes after it.
after: **In questions, the preposition moves to the front too:** *De que é que gostas?* — not *O que gostas?*. Portuguese prepositions can't be left dangling at the end of the sentence the way English ones can ("What do you like *about*?").
*Gostar de* also means "would like" in the polite form *gostaria de*: *Gostaria de ver o menu* — just as polite as *queria*.

grammars.title: The like-and-dislike scale
body: From strongest liking to strongest rejection. Notice which ones take *de* and which don't.
after: *Preferir* changes its vowel in the *eu* form, just like *dormir* in unit 9: **prefiro**, but *preferes*, *prefere*, *preferimos*, *preferem*.
To compare two things, *preferir* uses *a*: *Prefiro o chá ao café* (I prefer tea to coffee). Note *ao*, not *que* — much like English "prefer X *to* Y", not "than".

grammars.title: Pronouns after prepositions
body: After *para*, *de*, *com*, *em* and friends, pronouns take their own forms.
after: Only three forms are really new: *mim*, *ti*, *si*. The rest are the same as the normal forms.
Remember the special contractions with *com* from unit 8: *comigo*, *contigo*, *consigo*, *connosco* — not *com mim*.

blocks.text: *Ter razão* literally means "to have reason" — one more state expressed with *ter*, like *ter fome* in unit 5. The opposite: *não tens razão* or, more gently, *não sei se tens razão*.

blocks.title: Two words you need in Portugal
items: **Giro** is the everyday compliment you'll hear most in Portugal: for people, things, places, news — anything pleasant. *Que giro!* = "how cool!" In Brazil the word is hardly used in this sense.

**Chato** does two very different jobs: "boring" (*o filme é chato*) and "annoying" (*que chato!* = "oh, what a pity"). The second is actually heard more often, usually as a reaction to small bits of bad news.
Remember that adjectives for people always agree in gender: *ele é simpático*, *ela é simpática*.

exercises.prompt: Fill in de, do, da, dos or das.
Put the words in the right order.

items: I don't like the cold at all.
I think the food is good.

exercises.prompt: Spaced review — unit 9. Translate into Portuguese without looking back at the unit.
items: On Saturdays I sleep in late.

answers: de — da — dos — do — da — das
Não gosto nada de subir. — Acho que é ótimo. — Para mim é triste. — Prefiro o chá ao café. — De que é que gostas?
Gosto muito de Lisboa. — Não gosto nada do frio. — Acho que a comida é boa. — Para mim é caro demais. — Prefiro o chá ao café. — Tens razão.
Que horas são? — São sete e um quarto. — Estudo de manhã. — Ao sábado durmo até tarde. — Jantamos às oito.
